title: Columbine Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Columbine wells have a 40 ft median depth, but local records range to 1,948 ft. See yields, costs, risks and permit history.
h1: What to Know About Wells in Columbine, Colorado
intro_html:
Well records around Columbine show a wide range of conditions. The median reported depth is 40 feet, but the middle half runs from 25 to 249 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 1,948 feet. That spread matters when you compare a drilling bid or evaluate an existing home.

There are 3,534 wells in the Colorado DWR records within 5 miles of Columbine, although only 1,750 are recorded as constructed and 1,973 report a total depth. Use these records as local evidence, not as a guarantee for one lot. A nearby permit, well construction report, pump test and water-quality history are more useful than a regional average alone.

sections.heading: Columbine well depth depends on the local formation
sections.html:
Columbine sits on Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, and the records identify Denver Basin aquifers for 92% of wells. Many wells are shallow: 65% are under 100 feet. Another 13% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 14% between 300 and 600 feet, and 8% exceed 600 feet.

The 40-foot median should not be treated as a likely bid for every parcel. A middle-half range of 25 to 249 feet is a large spread for excavation and drilling planning. The 90th-percentile depth is 511 feet, while the deepest record is 1,948 feet. Have a driller review nearby completed wells, the target aquifer and the intended use before pricing a new hole.

sections.heading: Reported well yield is generally useful, but not uniform
sections.html:
Among the 267 wells that report a pump yield, the median is 12.0 gallons per minute. The middle half runs from 8.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Those figures are a reasonable local reference for a household discussion, but they are not a promise for an untested parcel.

Yield records show 48% producing between 5 and 15 gallons per minute and 37% producing more than 15 gallons per minute. Fourteen percent fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, while 1% are under 1 gallon per minute. Ask for the well’s actual pump test, storage capacity and permitted use. A low-yield well may still work with storage, but it gives a buyer less margin for irrigation or multiple occupants.

sections.heading: The Columbine water-level records do not show a simple drop
sections.html:
The median static water level is 24 feet below surface, with the middle half from 13 to 55 feet. That is the measured depth to water, not the total well depth. A shallow water level also does not by itself establish that the water is clean or that the well will sustain a given pumping rate.

By measurement decade, the median was 26 feet below surface in the 2010s and 15 feet in the 2020s. That change points to a shallower measured water level in the newer records, not a declining water table. Only 67 wells report a static water level, so do not use this series as a neighborhood-wide guarantee. Confirm current conditions with the owner’s well test and a qualified professional.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long use and continuing drilling
sections.html:
Permit records around Columbine extend through 2025. The largest decade in the record is the 1990s, with 702 permits, followed by 594 in the 2000s. The record includes 320 permits from the 2010s and 293 from the 2020s, along with earlier activity dating to the 1950s.

The most active names in the records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 985 entries; Hier Drilling Co Inc (Hier, Bruce A.), with 180; and Ground Exploration Llc (Bender, Joseph T.), with 88. These are record associations, not a recommendation or proof that a company is available today. Check the DWR permit, construction report, pump information and final use before relying on any listing.

sections.heading: A median-depth Columbine well pencils out at a specific range
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 40-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone models at about $2,000 to $2,800. That is only the drilling portion and should not be mistaken for a complete water system.

A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $8,000 to $14,800 at that median depth. Deeper-than-median drilling, difficult access, casing or grout requirements, water treatment and site-specific electrical work can change the bid. Ask for a written separation of drilling, casing, pump equipment, trenching, power and testing so competing bids cover the same work.

sections.heading: Columbine buyers need to check water, soil and site limits
sections.html:
Environmental screening within about 10 miles identifies 233 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 81 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites and 45 historic mine features. These mapped sites do not prove contamination at a particular address, but they are a reason to order current water-quality testing and review the well’s location, history and construction.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible because local records cover a broad depth range and only 267 wells report pump yield. Confirm the septic area, replacement septic area, setbacks, access for a drill rig and the location of the well relative to the house and drainfield. A Colorado DWR permit controls the allowed use; an exempt household-use well has specific limits, and an augmentation plan may be needed in an over-appropriated basin.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Columbine, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Columbine is 40 feet. The middle half of reported depths runs from 25 to 249 feet, while the 90th percentile is 511 feet. Records also include a deepest well of 1,948 feet. The broad range means nearby completed wells are more useful for estimating a new well than the median alone.

faq.q: What does a well cost to drill in Columbine?
faq.a: The local model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 40-foot median depth, the drilled hole models at about $2,000 to $2,800. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $8,000 to $14,800. A deeper hole, difficult access or added site work can change the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do Columbine wells produce?
faq.a: Of the 267 wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 12.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 8.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Forty-eight percent report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, while 1% report under 1 gallon per minute. Request the individual well’s pump test before buying.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Columbine?
faq.a: The regional records do not establish that water from a particular Columbine well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, mapped records include 233 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 81 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the actual well for the risks indicated by its location, and review construction and maintenance records.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Columbine?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a straightforward drop. Median static water level was 26 feet below surface in the 2010s and 15 feet in the 2020s, meaning the newer reported measurements were shallower. Only 67 wells report a static water level, so this limited series cannot predict conditions at every Columbine property.
